facts.text: Vitamin D helps the body absorb calcium, which is needed to build strong bones.
In children, a long-term lack of vitamin D can cause rickets, a disease in which bones become soft.
Few foods are rich in vitamin D; fatty fish such as salmon, tuna, and mackerel are among the best sources, and egg yolks contain smaller amounts.
The body makes vitamin D when bare skin is exposed to sunlight; a few minutes of sun on the arms or legs on most days may meet many people's needs, though output varies widely.
Only UVB light triggers vitamin D production in the skin; its strength depends on season, time of day, cloud cover, smog, and latitude.
UVB does not pass through window glass, so sitting in sunshine indoors behind a window does not produce vitamin D.
Darker skin and sunscreen can reduce vitamin D production, though studies disagree about how much sunscreen lowers vitamin D status in everyday use.
Longer unprotected sun exposure is not recommended because it raises the risk of skin cancer.
Studies of adolescents in Italy, Brazil, and China found low vitamin D levels to be common, with lower levels in winter.
In these studies, adolescents who spent more time active outdoors had better vitamin D status than those mainly active indoors.
